imo-2022-01.title: Count the blocks
imo-2022-01.body:
Call a maximal chain a *block*. The leftmost $n$ coins are all of one type exactly when the row has only $2$ blocks ($A^nB^n$ or $B^nA^n$). Write $M^b$ for a block of $b$ coins of type $M$.

**$k<n$ fails.** The row $A^{n-1}B^{n-1}AB$ has its $k$-th coin in the first block; moving that block to the left changes nothing, so the row never changes and always has $4$ blocks.

**$k>\lceil 3n/2\rceil$ fails.** Then $2k\ge 3n+2$. Put $a=k-n-1\ge1$ and $b=2n-k+1\ge1$, so $a+b=n$, and start from $A^aB^bA^bB^a$. A last block of size $s$ contains the $k$-th coin iff $k\ge 2n-s+1$; this holds for $s=b$ (equality) and for $s=a$ (it says $2k\ge3n+2$). So each operation moves the last block to the front:
$$A^aB^bA^bB^a\to B^aA^aB^bA^b\to A^bB^aA^aB^b\to B^bA^bB^aA^a\to A^aB^bA^bB^a\to\cdots,$$
and every row in this cycle has a last block of size $a$ or $b$. So there are always $4$ blocks.

**$n\le k\le\lceil3n/2\rceil$ works.** Suppose the row has $c\ge3$ blocks; we show the number of blocks never increases and eventually decreases.
- The moved block is not the first one: the first block has fewer than $n$ coins (otherwise it contains all $n$ coins of its type and $c=2$), so it does not contain position $k\ge n$.
- If a middle block is moved, its two neighbours (same type) merge, and placing the moved block at the front adds at most one block: the count drops by at least $1$.
- If the last block is moved and $c$ is odd, the first and last blocks have the same type, so it merges with the first block: the count drops by $1$.
- If the last block is moved and $c$ is even, the count stays the same and the sequence of blocks is rotated cyclically by one.

Suppose the count stayed equal to some even $c\ge4$ forever. Then the last block is moved every time, so after $c$ steps every block $a_1,\dots,a_c$ (sizes, $\sum a_i=2n$) has been last. Each time, $k\ge 2n+1-a_i$. Summing, $ck\ge c(2n+1)-2n$, so
$$k\ge 2n+1-\frac{2n}{c}\ge 2n+1-\frac n2=\frac{3n}2+1>\left\lceil\frac{3n}{2}\right\rceil,$$
a contradiction. Hence the number of blocks keeps decreasing until it reaches $2$, at which point the leftmost $n$ coins are of the same type.

**Answer:** all pairs with $n\le k\le\lceil 3n/2\rceil$.

imo-2022-02.title: Everyone is their own partner
imo-2022-02.body:
**$f(x)=1/x$ works:** $xf(y)+yf(x)=\frac xy+\frac yx\ge2$ with equality only for $y=x$, so $y=x$ is the unique solution.

Now let $f$ satisfy the condition. Call $y$ the *partner* of $x$ if $xf(y)+yf(x)\le2$. The condition is symmetric, so if $y$ is the partner of $x$ then $x$ is the partner of $y$, and everyone has exactly one partner.

**Claim: every $x$ is its own partner.** Suppose the partner of $a$ is $b\ne a$; then $b$'s partner is $a$. Since $a$ is not its own partner, $2af(a)>2$, i.e. $f(a)>\frac1a$; likewise $f(b)>\frac1b$. Then
$$2\ge af(b)+bf(a)>\frac ab+\frac ba\ge2,$$
a contradiction. $\square$

So for all $x$: $xf(x)\le1$, i.e. $f(x)\le\frac1x$; and for all $x\ne y$: $xf(y)+yf(x)>2$.

**Lower bound.** Fix $x$ and $\varepsilon>0$, and take $y=x+\varepsilon$. Using $f(x+\varepsilon)\le\frac1{x+\varepsilon}$,
$$2<xf(x+\varepsilon)+(x+\varepsilon)f(x)\le\frac{x}{x+\varepsilon}+(x+\varepsilon)f(x),$$
so
$$f(x)>\frac{2-\frac{x}{x+\varepsilon}}{x+\varepsilon}=\frac{x+2\varepsilon}{(x+\varepsilon)^2}.$$
Letting $\varepsilon\to0$ gives $f(x)\ge\frac1x$. Together with $f(x)\le\frac1x$, $f(x)=\frac1x$ for all $x$.

**Answer:** $f(x)=\frac1x$. ∎

imo-2022-03.title: Remove the largest prime
imo-2022-03.body:
Call an integer *good* if it equals $x^2+x+k$ for some integer $x\ge0$. Since $x^2+x+k=x'^2+x'+k$ for $x'=-1-x$, an integer is good iff it equals $x^2+x+k$ for some integer $x$. We prove the stronger statement where "positive" is replaced by "non-negative" (every arrangement in the original sense is also one in this sense), by induction on $|S|$. If $|S|\le3$ there is only one arrangement up to rotation and reflection.

**Claim 1.** Let $p$ be an odd prime. There are at most two primes $q<p$ such that $pq$ is good. If there are two, $q\ne r$, with $pq=x^2+x+k$ and $pr=y^2+y+k$, $x,y\ge0$, then $x+y+1=p$ and $xy\equiv k\pmod p$.

*Proof.* If $pq=x^2+x+k$ with $q<p$, then $x^2<pq<p^2$, so $0\le x\le p-1$, and $x$ is a root of $T^2+T+k$ modulo $p$. A quadratic has at most two roots modulo a prime, and $x$ determines $q=\frac{x^2+x+k}{p}$, so there are at most two such $q$. If there are two, $x\not\equiv y$ are the two roots, so $T^2+T+k\equiv(T-x)(T-y)$, giving $x+y\equiv-1$ and $xy\equiv k\pmod p$. As $x\ne y$ lie in $[0,p-1]$, $2\le x+y+1\le 2p-2$, hence $x+y+1=p$. $\square$

**Claim 2.** In that situation, $qr$ is good.

*Proof.* For integers $u,v$ one checks the identity
$$(x^2+x+k)(y^2+y+k)=u^2+uv+kv^2,\qquad u=xy-k,\ v=x+y+1$$
(it is the norm identity $N(x-\alpha)N(y-\alpha)=N\big((xy-k)-(x+y+1)\alpha\big)$ for a root $\alpha$ of $t^2+t+k$; it can also be verified by expanding). With $v=p$ and $u=xy-k=pz$ for an integer $z$:
$$p^2qr=p^2z^2+p^2z+kp^2,\qquad\text{so}\qquad qr=z^2+z+k,$$
which is good. $\square$

**Induction step.** Let $|S|\ge4$ and let $p$ be the largest element of $S$. In any valid arrangement, the two neighbours $q,r$ of $p$ are distinct primes in $S$ smaller than $p$ with $pq,pr$ good. By Claim 1 they are the only primes in $S\setminus\{p\}$ with this property, so the pair $\{q,r\}$ depends only on $S$. Removing $p$ from the circle makes $q$ and $r$ neighbours, and by Claim 2 the result is a valid arrangement of $S\setminus\{p\}$. By the induction hypothesis this arrangement is unique up to rotation and reflection, and the original one is recovered by inserting $p$ between the adjacent elements $q$ and $r$ (which are adjacent at exactly one place, as $|S\setminus\{p\}|\ge3$). Hence the arrangement of $S$ is unique as well. ∎

imo-2022-04.title: Similar triangles and a cyclic quadrilateral
imo-2022-04.body:
**Congruent triangles.** Since $TB=TD$, $TC=TE$ and $BC=DE$, the triangles $TBC$ and $TDE$ are congruent (SSS), so $\angle BTC=\angle DTE$.

**$\triangle TBQ\sim\triangle TES$.** The point $Q$ lies on line $CT$ beyond $T$ and $S$ on line $DT$ beyond $T$. So
$$\angle QTB=180^\circ-\angle BTC=180^\circ-\angle DTE=\angle ETS.$$
Moreover $Q$ is on ray $BA$ and $S$ is on ray $EA$, so $\angle TBQ=\angle TBA=\angle AET=\angle SET$. Two equal angles give $\triangle TBQ\sim\triangle TES$; in particular
$$\frac{TB}{TQ}=\frac{TE}{TS}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\angle BQT=\angle TSE.$$

**$C,D,Q,S$ are concyclic.** Using $TB=TD$ and $TE=TC$, the ratio becomes $\frac{TD}{TQ}=\frac{TC}{TS}$, i.e. $TD\cdot TS=TC\cdot TQ$. Since $T$ lies between $D$ and $S$ and between $C$ and $Q$, the converse of the power of a point gives that $C,D,Q,S$ are concyclic. Hence $\angle DCQ=\angle DSQ$.

**Angle chase.** On line $CD$ the order is $P,C,D,R$. In triangle $CPQ$, $\angle RCQ$ is the exterior angle at $C$, so
$$\angle RPQ=\angle CPQ=\angle RCQ-\angle PQC=\angle DCQ-\angle BQT.$$
Now $\angle DCQ=\angle DSQ$, and $\angle BQT=\angle TSE=\angle DSR$ (as $D$ lies on ray $ST$ and $R$ on ray $SE$). Therefore
$$\angle RPQ=\angle DSQ-\angle DSR=\angle RSQ.$$
The points $P$ and $S$ lie on the same side of line $QR$, so $P,S,Q,R$ are concyclic. ∎

imo-2022-05.title: Show $a=p$, then work mod $(p+1)^2$
imo-2022-05.body:
Both triples work: $2^2=2!+2$ and $3^3=27=4!+3$. Clearly $a\ge2$.

**Case $a<p$.** If $a\le b$, then $a\mid b!$ and $a\mid a^p$, so $a\mid p$, impossible for $1<a<p$. If $a>b$, then $b!\le a!<a^a\le a^{p-1}$, so $a^p-b!>a^p-a^{p-1}\ge 2^{p-1}\ge p$, contradicting $a^p-b!=p$.

**Case $a>p$.** Then $b!=a^p-p>p^p-p\ge p!$ (for $p\ge3$, $p!+p\le p^{p-1}+p<p^p$; for $p=2$, $p^p-p=2=p!$), so $b>p$. Then $p\mid b!+p=a^p$, so $p\mid a$ and $p^2\mid a^p$. Hence $b!=a^p-p\equiv -p\pmod{p^2}$ is not divisible by $p^2$, which forces $b<2p$.
- If $a<p^2$, write $a=pm$ with $1<m<p$. Then $m\le b$ divides $b!$ and $a^p$, so $m\mid p$, impossible.
- If $a\ge p^2$, then $a^p\ge p^{2p}$. But $(2p-1)!=p\prod_{i=1}^{p-1}i(2p-i)<p\cdot(p^2)^{p-1}=p^{2p-1}$, so $b!+p\le(2p-1)!+p<p^{2p-1}+p\le p^{2p}$, a contradiction.

**Case $a=p$.** Now $b!=p^p-p$.
- $p=2$: $b!=2$, so $b=2$: the triple $(2,2,2)$.
- $p=3$: $b!=24$, so $b=4$: the triple $(3,4,3)$.
- $p\ge5$: As above $b!=p^p-p>p!$, so $b\ge p+1$. Since $p\ge5$, the numbers $2$ and $\frac{p+1}2$ are distinct and at most $p$, so $p+1\mid p!$ and $(p+1)^2\mid(p+1)!\mid b!$. On the other hand, by the binomial theorem with $p=(p+1)-1$ and $p$ odd,
$$p^p\equiv\binom p1(p+1)(-1)^{p-1}+(-1)^p=p(p+1)-1\pmod{(p+1)^2},$$
so $p^p-p\equiv p^2-1=(p-1)(p+1)\pmod{(p+1)^2}$. This is not $\equiv0$, because $p+1\nmid p-1$ (as $0<p-1<p+1$). Contradiction.

**Answer:** $(a,b,p)=(2,2,2)$ and $(3,4,3)$.

imo-2022-06.title: Count paths ending at each cell; build a spanning comb
imo-2022-06.body:
**Counting.** For a cell $c$ let $N(c)$ be the number of uphill paths ending at $c$. A valley has no smaller neighbour, so $N(c)=1$. A non-valley cell is not itself an uphill path, and an uphill path ending at $c$ is an uphill path ending at a smaller neighbour $d$ of $c$, followed by $c$. Hence
$$N(c)=\sum_{d\sim c,\ d<c}N(d)\quad(c\text{ not a valley}).$$
Summing over all cells, the total number of uphill paths is
$$\#\{\text{valleys}\}+\sum_{\{c,d\}\text{ adjacent}}N(\text{smaller of }c,d).$$

**Lower bound.** The cell containing $1$ is a valley and every $N\ge1$. The board has $2n(n-1)$ adjacent pairs, so the total is at least $1+2n(n-1)=2n^2-2n+1$.

**Construction.** Equality needs exactly one valley and $N=1$ at the smaller cell of every adjacent pair. It suffices to find a set $T$ of cells such that (a) no two cells outside $T$ are adjacent, and (b) the cells of $T$ with their adjacencies form a tree. Given such $T$, list its cells so that each cell after the first is adjacent to an earlier one (e.g. breadth-first search from any cell of $T$) and write $1,2,\dots,|T|$ in that order; write the larger numbers in the other cells arbitrarily. Then:
- each cell of $T$ other than the first has exactly one smaller neighbour (its parent: its other $T$-neighbours are its children, which come later, and its neighbours outside $T$ are larger), and by induction $N=1$ on all of $T$;
- every cell outside $T$ has only neighbours in $T$, which are smaller; it is not a valley;
- so $1$ is the only valley, and the smaller cell of every adjacent pair lies in $T$ and has $N=1$. The total is exactly $2n^2-2n+1$.

**A suitable $T$.** Label rows $r=1,2,\dots$ from the top and columns by integers $j$. Let a cell $(r,j)$ be in $T$ when
- $j\equiv2\pmod6$ (any $r$); or $j\equiv5\pmod6$ and $r\ge2$;
- $j\equiv1,3\pmod6$ and $r$ odd;
- $j\equiv4,0\pmod6$ and ($r$ even or $r=1$).

So the columns $j\equiv2$ and $j\equiv5$ are "teeth" (vertical paths); the tooth in column $j\equiv2$ has side leaves in its two neighbouring columns on odd rows, and the tooth in column $j\equiv5$ (starting in row $2$) has side leaves on even rows; finally the connector cell $(1,j)$ with $j\equiv4$ joins the leaf $(1,j-1)$ of tooth $j-2$ to the leaf $(2,j)$ of tooth $j+1$, and the connector $(1,j)$ with $j\equiv0$ joins the leaf $(2,j)$ of tooth $j-1$ to the leaf $(1,j+1)$ of tooth $j+2$. (E.g. columns $1$–$6$: tooth $2$ with leaves $(1,1),(1,3),(3,1),(3,3),\dots$; connector $(1,4)$; tooth $5$ from row $2$ with leaves $(2,4),(2,6),(4,4),(4,6),\dots$; connector $(1,6)$ leading to $(1,7)$.)

*(a)* The cells outside $T$ are $(r\text{ even},\,j\equiv1,3)$, $(r\text{ odd}\ge3,\,j\equiv4,0)$ and $(1,\,j\equiv5)$. In each row these columns differ by at least $2$, and in each column they occur only in rows of one parity (or only in row $1$), so no two are adjacent.

*(b)* Each tooth with its leaves is a tree; leaves of different teeth are never adjacent (horizontally adjacent leaf columns use rows of opposite parity, and leaves in the same column are two rows apart), except through the row-$1$ connections, and consecutive teeth are joined by exactly one such connection. So $T$ is a tree.

For the $n\times n$ board use rows $1,\dots,n$ and columns $s,\dots,s+n-1$, with $s=1$ if $n\equiv0,2,3,5\pmod 6$ and $s=2$ if $n\equiv1,4\pmod6$. Then the last column is $\equiv 0,2,3$ or $5\pmod 6$, so cutting the pattern never leaves a leaf without its tooth; deleting the bottom rows and the outer columns keeps (a) and keeps $T$ connected and acyclic. (For instance $n=2$ gives the L-tromino $T=\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,2)\}$.)

**Answer:** $2n^2-2n+1$.
